sentences.text: Wimanius is a genus of ichthyosaur that contains only a single species, Wimanius odontopalatus.
This animal is recognized by its large eye socket and a jugal bone featuring two arms of equal length that meet at an 110-degree angle.
The species name odontopalatus highlights the unusual presence of teeth on the palate, where every tooth was straight, cone-shaped, and set into its own socket.
Scientists continue to disagree on whether these palate teeth sit on the palatine or pterygoid bone.
Reconstructions suggest Wimanius possessed the proportionally largest eye sockets of any Triassic ichthyosaur, resulting in a skull with a notably tall back.
Teeth located on the palate are a rare feature for ichthyosaurs, making this species unique among its peers.
Based on the size of the eye socket, researchers estimated the animal had a scleral ring containing 13 or 14 bony plates.
The genus was named in 1998 by Michael Maisch and Andreas Matzke after identifying an incomplete skull fragment while studying Mixosaurus fossils at the University of Tübingen.
The name Wimanius honors the Swedish paleontologist Carl Wiman for his contributions to the study of Triassic ichthyosaurs.
The lower jaw of the holotype specimen measures about 25 cm, indicating the animal was relatively small.
The only known specimen of Wimanius originates from the Besano Formation in Switzerland.
Surface waters in this habitat were well-oxygenated and rich in plankton and free-swimming organisms.
However, poor water circulation at the bottom of the lagoon led to anoxic conditions.
Fossils of conifers and land-dwelling reptiles indicate that Wimanius lived near land.
The bivalve Daonella was one of the most common invertebrates in the environment.
Cephalopods such as nautiloids, coleoids, and ammonites were also present in Wimanius' environment.
The habitat contained a diverse array of bony fish, including abundant small species and larger representatives like Saurichthys.
Cartilaginous fish were uncommon in the area and mainly consisted of hybodonts.
Other ichthyosaurs found in the same formation include Mixosaurus, Phalarodon, Besanosaurus, and Cymbospondylus.
Sauropterygians such as shell-crushing placodonts, pachypleurosaurs, and nothosaurids lived alongside Wimanius.
Marine reptiles like thalattosaurs and Tanystropheus coexisted with Wimanius in the Besano Formation.
The type species of the genus Wimanius is Wimanius odontopalatus.
Studies have placed Wimanius as a mixosaurid relative or a merriamosaur, and a family named Wimaniidae was created for it.
Motani classified Wimanius as Ichthyosauria incertae sedis in 1999.
Paul Martin Sander expressed doubt about the validity of Wimanius in 2000, suggesting further study was needed.
Maisch and Matzke considered Wimanius a valid taxon in 2000, placing it as the sister taxon of Mixosauridae.
Motani considered Wimanius and Mikadocephalus to be potential junior synonyms of Pessosaurus in 2003.
Only one fossil occurrence of Wimanius has been recorded.
Wimanius lived during the Late Triassic, specifically from the end of the Anisian to the beginning of the Ladinian stages.
The animal inhabited a marine lagoon in the western Tethys Ocean during the Late Triassic.
The marine lagoon where Wimanius lived was estimated to be between 30 and 130 meters deep.
The validity of Wimanius is debated, with some researchers suggesting it should be merged with other genera.
